Content:
I really hope that the sea water did get treated or, even better, simulated. Why? Florida tends to have a lotta issues with a diatom named Pseudo-nitzschia sp. Typically found in red algae blooms. (The Red Tide). This cause domoic acid poisoning in large quantities.  It is not killed by heat either. So boiling the water or cooking the meat is not effective.
Pseudo-nitzschia sp is water soluble to a degree, but can still inhabit the water, absorbing into the meat. So, if you are using sea water, please, PLEASE make sure it has been treated beyond boiling

Whether you use seawater or regular saltwater makes no difference at all. Thanks to osmotically assisted diffusion, the salt content will always regulate itself. You can even dry salt — the result will always be the same: the salt will distribute evenly throughout the entire piece of meat.

Smoked water is a bit different. Kombu does release MSG, but we all learned in kindergarten that oxides + water = acid. So you added, albeit slightly, an acid to the water, which broke down the connective tissue and gave the MSG that extra kick. Tender + umami.

Also, the gray edge and red center are no surprise. The pigment or corresponding protein is called myoglobin. That’s the stuff that turns into nitrosomyoglobin when cured with nitrite (curing salt)... basically the fake red in bacon, for example. It was, of course, washed out — but only to a certain depth. The longer the soak, the deeper it goes. Just don’t confuse washing out with osmotically assisted diffusion. The salt must be evenly distributed throughout — that’s a law of physics! But the pigment is only flushed out from the outside in, which takes significantly longer.

In other words: you put one steak in regular saltwater and another in MSG-infused acid. What did you expect would happen?

Author: @bgmkaak
Content:
MSG was made by kombu in the past, nowdays it is made by gmo corn. 

The production of monosodium glutamate (MSG) has evolved significantly over time. Here's a breakdown of how MSG was made in the past versus today:

Past MSG Production (Early 1900s – mid-20th century)
1. Extraction from natural sources:

Source: MSG was originally derived from seaweed, particularly kombu (a type of kelp).

Method: In 1908, Japanese scientist Kikunae Ikeda discovered MSG by extracting glutamic acid from kombu using water, filtering, and evaporation.

Yield: The process was inefficient and yielded small amounts of MSG, making it costly.

2. Chemical synthesis (mid-20th century):

As demand increased, producers shifted to chemical methods.

Process: Glutamic acid was produced through chemical hydrolysis of proteins (like wheat gluten or casein), then neutralized with sodium to form MSG.

Downside: More industrial but less sustainable and sometimes criticized for harsh processing.

Modern MSG Production (1970s – Present)
1. Fermentation process (biotechnology):

Current standard method.

Source: Uses sugar-rich feedstocks like sugarcane, corn, or molasses.

Microorganisms: Specific strains of Corynebacterium or other bacteria ferment the sugars and naturally secrete glutamic acid.

The glutamic acid is then isolated and combined with sodium to make MSG.

Benefits:

More efficient and sustainable.

Mimics natural processes (like those in food fermentation).

Considered "natural" under many food regulations.
